messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 42
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Tax Inspector
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 72

Rajesh is a forty-two-year-old tax inspector who has been coming to see me for the past six weeks. He sits at the edge of the armchair, hands pressed flat on his thighs as if bracing for impact. He speaks in short, careful sentences, but his eyes betray a constant scanning—the door, the window, my face, the door again.

The accident happened eight months ago, on a rainy Thursday evening in late November. Rajesh had just finished auditing a small retail chain—a routine compliance visit in a part of the city he rarely drove. He was tired, eager to get home to his wife and two children. The road was slick, the wipers struggling against the downpour. He remembers a blurred shape darting from between two parked cars. The thud. The screech. The impossible stillness of the man lying on the asphalt.

Rajesh stopped immediately. He called emergency services, knelt beside the man, and held his hand until the ambulance arrived. The man—forty-five, a factory worker named Mr. Chowdhury—suffered a severe traumatic brain injury, a broken pelvis, and internal bleeding. He survived, but he will never walk again without assistance. The police report cleared Rajesh of any fault; the man had been intoxicated and crossed against the light. But for Rajesh, fault is not a legal question.

In the weeks that followed, he could not sleep. He replayed the moment—the wet road, the shadow, the thud—on a loop inside his head. He visited Mr. Chowdhury at the hospital once, carrying a basket of fruit he could not bring himself to offer. He stood at the door, saw the tubes and the bandages, and walked away. He has not been back.

Now, Rajesh lives inside a body that no longer feels his own. He avoids driving the route where the accident happened. He takes the bus to work, a journey that adds nearly an hour to his commute. When the bus moves through that part of the city, he presses his face toward the window and breathes shallowly, willing himself not to look for the exact spot. He never looks.

At the tax office, Rajesh was once known for his efficiency and calm demeanor. He handled complex audits, mediated disputes, and met deadlines without fuss. Now, he double- and triple-checks every form, every line item, every signature. He cannot trust his own eyes. He fears that one overlooked detail will cause another catastrophe—a wrong assessment, a penalty imposed unfairly, another life disrupted by his hand. His supervisor has noticed. Rajesh has been warned about his declining pace. He does not explain why.

His wife, Meera, tries to reach him. She cooks his favorite dishes, leaves tea in his study, asks gentle questions about his day. He answers in monosyllables. When she touches his shoulder, he flinches. He does not mean to. His body acts before his mind catches up. They have not been intimate in months. He knows she feels rejected. He sees her hurt in the way she turns away at night, pulling the blanket to her side of the bed. But he cannot explain the leaden weight in his chest, the sense that he has no right to joy.

At night, the accident finds him again. He dreams of the thud—a sound that has no volume but fills every corner of his skull. He wakes gasping, drenched in sweat, heart hammering. He lies still, listening to Meera’s breathing beside him, and wonders if Mr. Chowdhury is also awake, staring at a hospital ceiling. He has searched Mr. Chowdhury’s name online, read the news articles, looked at the crowdfunding page his family set up. He has never donated. He cannot bring himself to type his own name.

During the day, Rajesh is hypervigilant without knowing it. Pedestrians near the curb make his stomach clench. A sudden honk on the street sends his heart racing. At work, the ringing phone makes him drop his pen. He has begun snapping at colleagues for small mistakes—a misplaced decimal, a late file—and then feels a wash of shame. He once prided himself on patience. Now he is a stranger to himself.

Meera has started leaving books about trauma on his nightstand. He has not opened them. He tells himself he does not deserve explanations, or forgiveness. He is not a bad man. But he believes, in the hollow of his chest, that he is irreparably broken.
